physical_harm: Victim-deceased succumbed to injuries; PW-1 and PW-2 sustained injuries
premeditation_planning: Yes, A-11 instigated others to cut the deceased into pieces
motive: Taking life of the deceased, based on history of earlier attack
key_evidence_accepted: The oral testimony of material witnesses PW-1 and PW-2 was corroborated by the medical evidence, whereas the motive of taking life of the deceased was made out from the incident.
witness_credibility: Some contradictions arose on account of perception of the witnesses and due to passage of time. But the creditability of the witnesses was not shaken. Therefore, such witnesses were reliable and creditworthy.

legal_representation.accused: P. B. Suresh, Vipin Nair, Karthik Jayashankar, Advs.
legal_representation.state: M. Yogesh Kanna, Ms. Meha Aggarwal, Partha Sarathi, S. Raja Rajeshwaran, Advs.

investigation_status: FIR lodged on April 26, 2003, trial completed
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that there was a history of previous attack on the complainant party, and on the fateful day, all the accused armed with weapons surrounded PW-1, PW-2 and the deceased. A-11 instigated the other accused to cut the victim-deceased into pieces, leading to the deceased succumbing to injuries. The prosecution also emphasized the medical evidence corroborating the oral testimony of PW-1 and PW-2, and the motive of taking life of the deceased was made out from the incident.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the so-called injured witnesses PW-1 and PW-2 were introduced by the prosecution and their injuries were not proved to be inflicted by the accused. They also contended that the statements of these witnesses were contradictory and that the prosecution failed to prove a common object to commit murder, relying on precedents such as Ram Laxman v. State of Rajasthan and Najabhai Desurbhai Wagh v. Valerabhai Deganbhai Vagh & Ors.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that the cumulative effect of the evidence led by the prosecution determines whether an unlawful assembly had a common object to commit culpable homicide amounting to murder. It also reiterated that the maxim 'falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus' has no application in India, and the rule of caution is required when examining the statements of witnesses whose part statement is not found to be truthful.
precedent_relied_upon: Ram Laxman v. State of Rajasthan (2016) 12 SCC 389; Najabhai Desurbhai Wagh v. Valerabhai Deganbhai Vagh & Ors. (2017) 3 SCC 261; Mahendran v. State of Tamil Nadu (2019) 5 SCC 67
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed based on the cumulative effect of the evidence led by the prosecution, which established that the accused formed an unlawful assembly with a view to take the life of the deceased, and that the findings recorded by the courts below were plausible findings in law.
